paper.title: ClinicalAge, a framework for modelling ageing trajectories from longitudinal electronic health records in the UK: a model development and validation study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Ageing is a key determinant of morbidity and mortality. In this study, we aimed to develop and assess a new ageing biomarker, ClinicalAge, derived from routinely collected longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data.
Methods: In this model development and validation study, we used UK Biobank data for model development and UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) Aurum data for model validation. The UK Biobank is a longitudinal population-based cohort of approximately 500 000 individuals aged 40-69 years at recruitment (March 16, 2006, to Oct 1, 2010), with linked EHR from the November 2022 UK Biobank data release. CPRD Aurum is a primary care EHR database containing anonymised longitudinal data from over 30 million patients across the UK, including diagnoses, medication, procedures, and laboratory results. A transformer-based deep learning model was trained from longitudinal EHR data to generate ClinicalAge using the validated biomarker PhenoAge as reference. We used a UK Biobank cohort for model development and internal validation, and three CPRD Aurum cohorts for external validation, longitudinal trajectory analysis, and comparison with the electronic frailty index. ClinicalAge was evaluated for associations with 17 functional measures, ten biological ageing biomarkers, 31 ageing-related diseases (11 cancer diagnoses and 20 non-cancer diseases), and all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality. We further examined longitudinal ClinicalAge trajectories and investigated clinical and disease-specific factors associated with accelerated ageing.
Findings: The UK Biobank cohort included 320 891 participants (median chronological age 58·0 years [IQR 51·0-63·0]; median PhenoAge 56·0 years [48·6-62·0]; 173 067 [53·9%] were female; and 147 824 [46·1%] were male) and the CPRD cohort included 4 728 376 individuals (51·0 years [44·0-60·0]; 2 293 243 [48·5%] were female and 2 435 133 [51·5%] were male). ClinicalAge had an R2 score of 0·819 with PhenoAge and showed a significant association with the 17 functional measures and ten biological ageing biomarkers. It was also significantly associated with the incidence of all 20 non-cancer diseases in both datasets, as well as nine (82%) of 11 cancers in UK Biobank (seven positive associations and two negative) and ten (91%) of 11 cancers (eight positive associations and two negative) in CPRD. Moreover, ClinicalAge was significantly associated with all-cause mortality (UK Biobank adjusted hazard ratio [HR] 1·23 [95% CI 1·21-1·24]; CPRD adjusted HR 1·36 [1·36-1·36]), cancer mortality (UK Biobank adjusted HR 1·12 [1·10-1·14]; CPRD adjusted HR 1·17 [1·16-1·17]), and cardiovascular mortality (UK Biobank adjusted HR 1·33 [1·29-1·36]; CPRD adjusted HR 1·36 [1·35-1·36]), after adjustment for clinical covariates and lifestyle factors. Midlife was identified as a key window for divergence, with early acceleration in individuals developing diabetes, hypertension, depression, or lifestyle disorders.
Interpretation: ClinicalAge is a non-invasive biomarker that leverages routinely collected EHR data to quantify ageing across the life course. It shows strong associations with ageing-related biomarkers, functional decline, disease risk, and mortality. Its interpretability and anticipatory signal offer a practical tool for the early identification of individuals at risk of accelerated ageing, enabling targeted preventive strategies such as lifestyle modification, cardiometabolic control, and mental health support.
Funding: None.

paper.title: Interpreting and Validating a Deep Learning Model Predictive of Spatial Morphologic-Molecular Patterns in Lung Adenocarcinoma, Using Ground Truth Immunohistochemistry Images.
paper.abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, exhibits profound histological and molecular heterogeneity. While genomic profiling has identified key oncogenic drivers and immune signatures, its use is limited by cost, technical demands and tissue availability. In addition, spatial transcriptomics provides spatially resolved molecular insights but remains challenging and time-consuming. To address this gap, we developed XpressO-Lung, an explanatory deep learning model that predicts gene expression heterogeneity spatially in tumor and its microenvironment on hematoxylin and eosin based diagnostic (Dx) whole-slide images (WSIs) by learning associations between tissue morphology and the corresponding bulk-transcriptomic data. Utilizing 200 LUAD cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas, XpressO-Lung predicted spatial expression patterns of NAPSA, TP53I3, CD8A, TTF1, KRT7, CDKN2A, FOXO1, KEAP1, RB1 and TP53 on Dx-WSIs with AUCs ranging from 0.64 to 0.92. The predicted spatial gene expression patterns aligned with the known morphologic interactions of the tumor and its microenvironment, capturing biological events directly on Dx-WSIs. These spatio-morpho-molecular associations were further validated using immunohistochemistry on an external set of clinical samples at Dartmouth Health, demonstrating concordance between model-predicted spatial patterns and observed histomorphologic features. By coupling predictive performance with spatial interpretability of gene expression on Dx-WSIs, the XpressO-Lung model bridges histopathology and bulk-transcriptomics, enabling explainable spatio-morpho-genomic analyses to advance biomarker discovery, therapeutic stratification and precision oncology in LUAD.

paper.title: Expanding tobacco dependency service reach through AI-assisted identification of hospital inpatients who smoke: A prospective study.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: Tobacco smoking remains a major public health challenge, and the NHS Long Term Plan commits hospitals to identifying and treating tobacco dependency in all admitted patients who smoke. Systematic identification of patients who smoke within hospitals is limited by incomplete structured electronic health record (EHR) data, leaving many patients unreferred to cessation support. Natural language processing (NLP) offers a means of identifying smoking status from unstructured clinical text. We evaluated the impact of an AI-assisted referral pathway on tobacco dependency service delivery during routine clinical deployment.
Study Design: Prospective 12-week study in a large London acute NHS trust. ClinicalSmokeBERT, an NLP model developed to classify smoking status from EHR free text, scanned clinical notes daily to identify patients who currently smoke, generating referrals alongside the standard structured-data pathway.
Methods: The primary outcome measure was the total number of referrals contributed by each pathway. Secondary outcomes assessed referral quality between pathways using a non-inferiority framework with a 15-percentage-point margin: positive predictive value (PPV, defined as the proportion of patients seen by a tobacco dependency advisor who were confirmed as currently smoking) and clinical engagement (proportion of patients confirmed as currently smoking who accepted support). Patients not seen by an advisor were not included in the secondary analyses because their smoking status could not be verified.
Results: The AI pathway nearly doubled referrals to the tobacco dependency service (99.6% increase relative to the non-AI standard care pathway). Referral quality was broadly similar, with high clinical engagement among patients confirmed as currently smoking (AI:89.2% vs non-AI:85.0%), while non-inferiority for PPV was not demonstrated (AI:66.0% vs non-AI:77.1%). No significant sociodemographic differences were observed between pathways, indicating no evidence of model bias.
Conclusions: AI-assisted identification of inpatients who smoke extends tobacco dependency service reach without compromising referral quality or introducing demographic bias, supporting its role as an additive component of routine clinical pathways.

paper.title: Peri-ablational contrast-enhanced CT radiomics for predicting early progression of hepatocellular carcinoma after microwave ablation: development and external validation of a clinical-radiomics model.
paper.abstract:
Purpose: To develop and externally validate a peri-ablational contrast-enhanced CT radiomics model for predicting early hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression after microwave ablation (MWA) and to assess its incremental value over clinical predictors.
Methods: This retrospective multicenter study included 376 patients in training (n = 235), internal validation (n = 60), and external validation (n = 81) cohorts. Early progression was defined as local tumor progression or new intrahepatic HCC within 1 year after MWA. Radiomics features were extracted from 5-mm peri-ablational regions on multiphasic CT obtained 1-2 months after MWA. Six machine-learning algorithms and phase combinations were evaluated. The selected radiomics model was combined with independent clinical predictors. Discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and model interpretability were assessed.
Results: The arterial-plus-portal venous phase (AP + PP) multilayer perceptron model achieved AUCs of 0.857, 0.815, and 0.903 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively, with performance comparable to the three-phase model. Log10 AFP and tumor size > 2 cm were independent clinical predictors. The combined clinical-radiomics model achieved AUCs of 0.926, 0.884, and 0.963, respectively. In external validation, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 84.2%, 96.8%, and 93.8%, respectively. SHAP analysis identified the radiomics score as the most influential predictor.
Conclusion: Peri-ablational AP + PP CT radiomics combined with AFP and tumor size demonstrated good discrimination for early HCC progression after MWA and may facilitate individualized risk assessment, pending further validation.

paper.title: An interpretable machine learning model using routine clinical indicators for early pediatric sepsis risk stratification: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Sepsis remains a leading cause of pediatric morbidity and mortality worldwide. The 2024 Phoenix Sepsis Criteria emphasize early recognition of organ dysfunction. Conventional diagnostics like blood cultures are time-consuming, and existing machine learning models lack early pathogen-level classification. A machine learning framework for early pediatric sepsis warning and Gram-stain pathogen classification was developed and validated using routine clinical indicators.
Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included 784 children: 432 from Fujian Children's Hospital for model development and 352 from the Pediatric Intensive Care database of the Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine for external-cohort evaluation. From 56 clinical variables and 9 derived indices, features were selected in the training cohort by univariable analysis, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) evaluation. Eight algorithms were compared, with external-cohort accuracy also informing hyperparameter selection. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret predictions. The Gram-stain nomogram was developed and evaluated in the pathogen-confirmed training sub-cohort.
Results: The reported models used 12 features. Random forest achieved an AUC of 0.887 (95% confidence interval: 0.850-0.924) and accuracy of 82.1% in the external cohort. Decision curve analysis suggested potential clinical net benefit. C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, alanine aminotransferase, and white blood cell count contributed most to model output. SHAP plots described nonlinear associations within the fitted model. The exploratory Gram-stain nomogram achieved an apparent AUC of 0.753 (95% confidence interval: 0.661-0.844) in the development sub-cohort, with sensitivity of 57.1% and specificity of 80.3% for Gram-positive infection.
Conclusion: The random forest model showed potential for early pediatric sepsis risk stratification and warrants evaluation in an independent cohort. The Gram-stain nomogram provides exploratory findings that require external validation before clinical use. Antibiotic selection and de-escalation should be guided by microbiological evidence and comprehensive clinical assessment.

paper.title: Analysis of prognostic factors for survival after curative resections of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma based on Bayesian networks.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate risk stratification following curative resection of non-metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (nm-ccRCC) remains clinically challenging. This study aims to develop and validate Bayesian network (BN) models to predict survival in patients with nm-ccRCC.
Methods: A dual-center retrospective cohort was randomly stratified into a training set (N = 326) and an internal validation set (N = 140). External validation was performed using an independent external cohort (N = 170). BN models were constructed based on clinicopathologic characteristics that demonstrated statistical significance in univariate analyses of the training cohort and were assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, confusion matrices, calibration and decision curve analysis.
Results: The Bayesian analyses identified T stages as the principal determinant of 5-year overall survival (OS), while ISUP grades emerged as the dominant predictor for 3-year disease-free survival (DFS). The 5-year OS and 3-year DFS models achieved areas under the ROC curve (AUCs) of 0.878 and 0.867 in the internal validation cohort and 0.838 and 0.846 in the external validation cohort. Calibration slopes were close to unity with small intercepts across cohorts, and decision curve analysis showed net benefit exceeding that of treating all or no patients across a wide range of thresholds.
Conclusions: This study establishes BNs for the first time as a clinically actionable tool for postoperative risk prediction in nm-ccRCC, with promising discriminative and calibrated performance supporting their potential use in patient counseling, risk-stratified surveillance, and the selection of candidates for adjuvant therapy or clinical trials. Future prospective, multicenter studies are warranted to extend these predictions to a 5-year DFS endpoint and to refine the decision threshold for clinical translation.

paper.title: Clinical validation of the Swaasa® artificial intelligence platform using cough sounds for screening and aid in diagnosis of respiratory diseases.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: Cough sound analysis can provide clues to underlying respiratory disease. The Swaasa AI platform, a Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), applies artificial intelligence to cough recordings to generate indications, including overall risk (normal vs. abnormal), spirometric pattern (obstructive, restrictive, or normal), pattern severity (mild, moderate, severe), and the presence of asthma, COPD, ILD, and bronchiectasis.
Methods: Patients (≥18 years) presenting to our departments with respiratory symptoms were prospectively recruited. Cough sounds were recorded on a mobile device running the Swaasa AI platform, spirometry was performed. Spirometry served as the reference standard for physiological pattern and severity, while physician-established clinical diagnosis served as the reference for disease categories. Polychotomous variables were dichotomized as normal vs. abnormal, & multi-class output for disease condition, pattern severity, and disease categories (asthma, COPD, ILD, bronchiectasis) were defined.
Trial Registration: CTRI/2021/04/032742; registered on 12/04/2021; date of first enrollment: 19/04/2021; trial end date: 14/09/2023.
Results: We recruited 2,179 patients with respiratory diseases and 827 normal individuals; 62% were male. The Swaasa AI platform achieved 90% accuracy in distinguishing normal from abnormal (respiratory condition present) and in classifying normal vs. abnormal spirometry, with descriptive performance subgroup analyses showing broadly comparable performance across age and gender groups For multi-class outcomes, the accuracy ranges were: spirometry pattern: 79%-84%, pattern severity: 76%-84.5%, and disease-type classification: 83%-93%.
Conclusion: Swaasa® demonstrates promising performance in distinguishing normal from abnormal respiratory conditions across demographic subgroups, indicating its promise as a screening tool. While the accuracy measures emphasize further refinement to ensure consistent high performance across specific respiratory disease scenarios and severity levels, the study shows its reasonable potential in identifying specific respiratory diseases and their severity.

paper.title: Deep learning-powered virtual eosin-based elastic fiber framework imaging improves objective grading and prognostic stratification of lung adenocarcinoma.
paper.abstract:
Background: Histological grading of lung adenocarcinoma is limited by interobserver variability, particularly when distinguishing noninvasive lepidic growth from invasive patterns. This distinction depends on evaluation of the alveolar elastic fiber framework, which is often insufficiently visualized on routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides.
Methods: We developed a deep learning framework to improve grading objectivity by computationally visualizing elastic fiber-related architecture from standard H&E images. A dual-stream EfficientNet-B0 classifier was trained using spatially coregistered H&E and eosin-based elastin fluorescence (EBEF) images. To enable clinical deployment without additional staining or fluorescence microscopy, a Pix2Pix-HD generative adversarial network was trained to synthesize high-fidelity virtual EBEF images from H&E alone. The resulting automated pipeline classified histological patterns, quantified pattern proportions, and assigned tumor grades. Performance was evaluated on independent multicenter cohorts, with ablation analyses assessing key pipeline components. Prognostic relevance was explored using a curated TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort.
Results: The benchmark dual-stream model using real H&E and EBEF achieved 89.3% tile-level classification accuracy. Using virtual EBEF images, the automated grading pipeline achieved 94.2% accuracy on an external validation cohort, outperforming an H&E-only model (79.6%). Ablation studies confirmed that performance gains depended on informative multimodal input, accurate spatial registration, and attentive feature fusion. AI-assigned grades demonstrated a consistent trend toward association with overall survival in TCGA, with significant stratification observed when low-grade tumors were combined (log-rank p = 0.048).
Conclusions: This framework enables objective grading of lung adenocarcinoma from a single routine H&E slide by enhancing visualization of elastic fiber-related architecture. The approach improves grading consistency and prognostic stratification without altering standard pathology workflows.

paper.title: Early prediction of novel dynamic subphenotypes in acute pancreatitis with hypertriglyceridemia: a multicenter cohort study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Concomitant with the escalating global burden of metabolic disorders, acute pancreatitis with hypertriglyceridemia (AP-HTG) has become highly prevalent. However, the initial triglyceride elevation does not strictly correlate with adverse clinical outcomes. Therefore, we aimed to identify novel dynamic subphenotypes reflecting the intrinsic pathophysiological state and develop an early prediction model.
Methods: Clinicopathological data were collected from MIMIC-IV (n = 344, development), eICU-CRD (n = 173, external validation), and an independent local cohort (n = 319, pragmatic validation). Group-based multi-trajectory modeling (GBMTM) of 7-day white blood cell and calcium trajectories was utilized to identify novel subphenotypes. After evaluating multiple machine-learning algorithms, an optimal early prediction model was established using Boruta, LASSO, and logistic regression based on admission-day indicators.
Results: Four novel dynamic subphenotypes were identified, with the Severe-Hyperinflammatory (C3) and Lipotoxic-Hypocalcemic (C4) subphenotypes carrying substantially increased independent risks for persistent organ failure and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome. Furthermore, an early logistic regression prediction model comprising white blood cells, calcium, lymphocytes, albumin, platelets, and hematocrit was developed. This model achieved high macro-average AUCs in the development (0.924) and external validation (0.933) cohorts. Pragmatic validation in the local cohort further confirmed its utility in effectively identifying high-risk subphenotypes. To enhance interpretability and clinical utility, SHAP analysis was applied, and the model was deployed as a free web-based calculator and a nomogram specifically designed for the C4 subphenotype.
Conclusions: This study identified four novel dynamic AP-HTG subphenotypes and developed a multicenter-validated early prediction model using admission-day indicators. It facilitates early risk stratification and individualized clinical decision-making.

paper.title: Interpretable machine learning models for early prediction of all-cause mortality in patients with traumatic brain injury combined with venous thromboembolism: a retrospective study.
paper.abstract:
Background: To develop and validate interpretable machine learning (ML) models for predicting all-cause mortality in critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury combined with venous thromboembolism using data from the US-based Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) and eICU databases.
Methods: Data from 321 patients with TBI and VTE were extracted from the MIMIC-IV database and split into training (70%) and validation (30%) sets. Fifty-five variables, including demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, and medical scores, were analyzed using the Boruta algorithm to identify predictors of in-hospital, 30-day, and 90-day mortality. Nine machine learning algorithms were evaluated, with the best-performing model validated using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) database. Model performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), while accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, Kappa value etc. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was used to interpret the model.
Results: The Boruta algorithm identified 6, 5, and 7 predictors for in‑hospital, 30‑day, and 90‑day mortality, respectively. Among nine ML models, multilayer perceptron (MLP) performed favorable for in‑hospital mortality (AUROC 0.758, accuracy 0.919, specificity 0.948, PPV 0.500, F1 0.545, Kappa 0.50). Light gradient‑boosting machine (LightGBM) was optimal for 30‑day mortality (AUROC 0.794, accuracy 0.801, specificity 0.873, NPV 0.901). Logistic regression performed favorable for 90‑day mortality (AUROC 0.791, sensitivity 0.818, NPV 0.926). Top features: in‑hospital: age, diastolic blood pressure min, potassium max, blood urea nitrogen (BUN) max, sodium min; 30‑day: glucose min, potassium max, glucose max, BUN min, BUN max; 90‑day: age, sodium min, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) min, heart failure, gender. In external validation, MLP achieved AUROC 0.717 (0.621-0.813) for in‑hospital mortality, LightGBM 0.529 (0.410-0.649) for 30‑day, and logistic regression 0.691 (0.588-0.795) for 90‑day mortality.
Conclusion: The results indicated that the MLP model performed well for predicting in-hospital mortality. The LightGBM model showed favorable performance in predicting 30-day mortality, while logistic regression presented good discriminatory ability for 90-day mortality. Additionally, SHAP analysis identified maximum potassium and maximum BUN as shared key indicators for in-hospital and 30-day mortality, whereas age and low serum sodium were critical factors associated with in-hospital and 90-day mortality risks. Future work should focus on validating the model in diverse populations and incorporating additional clinical data to enhance its applicability.
Trial Registration: Not applicable.

paper.title: Ultrasound-guided deep learning framework with whole slide images for molecular subtyping of breast cancer: a multicentre, retrospective study.
paper.abstract: Accurate molecular subtyping of breast cancer is essential for personalized therapy, yet inconsistencies between biopsy and postoperative immunohistochemistry (IHC) due to tumor heterogeneity and sampling limitations pose clinical challenges. We developed Ultrasound-Guided Pathomic Subtyping (US-GPS), a cross-modal framework enabling subtype prediction using ultrasound (US) alone, guided by IHC-stained whole-slide images (WSIs) during training. A total of 1283 patients from four centers were retrospectively included, with 454 cases (paired US and WSIs) for model training/validation and 829 US-only cases for external testing. US-GPS aligned WSI-derived patch- and region-level features (from HER2, ER, PR, Ki-67 IHC stains) with handcrafted and deep US features via co-attention and contrastive learning. Using US alone, the model achieved an AUROC of 0. 966 (95% CI 0.960-0.991) in internal validation, comparable to pathology-only (0. 971) and joint models (0.980), and superior to US-only (0.861). Performance remained robust across both internal (AUROC range: 0.930-0.942) and all external cohorts (AUROC range: 0.915-0.963). US-GPS enables scalable, non-invasive, and interpretable subtype classification, with potential for both pre-treatment decision-making and longitudinal monitoring of molecular phenotypic shifts.

paper.title: Development and clinical validation of a multiplex PCR-based targeted next-generation sequencing panel for simultaneous DNA/RNA pathogen detection in respiratory tract infections: a comprehensive performance evaluation.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI) remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, with approximately 62 % of cases lacking definitive etiological diagnoses via conventional methods. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiplex PCR-based targeted next-generation sequencing (mp-tNGS) panel for comprehensive pathogen detection in respiratory samples.
Methods: We conducted a combined retrospective (n=209) and prospective (n=256) study involving 465 bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) samples from patients with suspected LRTI. The mp-tNGS panel was designed to detect 277 clinically relevant pathogens, integrating simultaneous DNA/RNA co-detection and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based contamination control. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against conventional microbiological tests (CMTs) and metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS).
Results: The mp-tNGS assay revealed a limit of detection (LoD) of 25 copies/mL for bacteria/fungi and 50 copies/mL for viruses, with acceptable precision (intrabatch CV=9.42 %; interbatch CV=26.03 %). A novel SNP-based bioinformatics pipeline achieved exceptional discriminative performance (AUC=0.992) for distinguishing true infections from contamination. Compared with CMTs and mNGS, mp-tNGS showed superior sensitivity (93.59 %, 95 % CI: 90.81-95.73 %), particularly for viruses (AUC=0.92 vs. 0.845). The assay reliably identified fastidious pathogens (e.g., Pneumocystis jirovecii and Legionella pneumophila) and predicted antimicrobial resistance (97.08 % concordance with phenotypic testing).
Conclusions: We developed an mp-tNGS panel with diagnostic performance comparable to that of mNGS. The panel integrates broad pathogen coverage, rapid turnaround time, machine learning-based false-positive reduction, and concordance with phenotypic susceptibility testing, positioning it as a promising molecular diagnostic tool for LRTI.
